climbing_route.label: South snowfield from Perfect Pass
climbing_route.notes: From camp at Perfect Pass the route heads north and up onto the broad south-side snowfield, which is the lower margin of the Whatcom Glacier. The angle is moderate and the line is obvious, aiming for the conspicuous col in the summit ridge above. Ice axe is standard and crampons are usual on firm morning snow. Because this is glacier ice under the seasonal snow, early-season parties treat it as glacier travel; later in the year the cover thins and moats open along the rock margin where the snow meets the summit block. Reports describe it as long but straightforward, roughly an hour from the pass.

climbing_route.label: Col in the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: The snowfield is left at the obvious col on the summit ridge. Some parties instead break out onto ramps and ledges to the northeast of the col and rejoin the crest higher. The transition from snow to rock is where a moat or a lip of hard snow is most likely to be awkward, and it is worse late in the season.

climbing_route.label: South ridge crest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: The final stretch along the crest is short — on the order of a hundred feet — but very exposed, with drops on both sides. The rock here is described as poor quality and protection opportunities are limited, so a light rack and slings are carried and many parties belay this section even though the moves are only third to fourth class. The route as a whole is generally graded fourth class on account of this last bit; the scrambling itself is described as enjoyable rather than difficult, with the exposure and the loose rock being the real concerns. Descent reverses the line, and on good snow the return to Perfect Pass is very quick.

climbing_route.label: Sisters Glacier to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle between North Twin's southeast ridge and South Twin's north ridge, the route gains the crest by way of the Sisters Glacier and the snow on the north side of the ridge. In early summer coverage is generally good, crevasses are buried and snow bridges are reported as solid, but this is glacier travel and should be treated as such. The moat where the snow meets rock is the recurring obstacle and it widens through the season; parties late in the year find the glacier shrunken and the moat, rather than the crevasses, the thing that stops them. Ice axe and crampons are standard, with pickets or flukes carried early season.

climbing_route.label: Lower and middle crest
climbing_route.notes: Sustained third-class scrambling with occasional fourth-class steps up the ridge crest. The rock is dunite, an olivine-rich ultramafic rock, and it is exceptionally grippy and solid — commonly compared to coarse sandpaper — which makes the scrambling pleasant but does not remove the exposure, which is continuous. A minimal rack is usual for this section; most parties move unroped here.

climbing_route.label: High notch around 6,600 ft
climbing_route.notes: A distinct notch breaks the ridge at roughly 6,600 ft. This is the natural decision point: above it the character of the route changes, and it is where parties choose between staying on the crest and taking the south-side bypass.

climbing_route.label: Final crest, last 400 ft
climbing_route.notes: The last four hundred vertical feet on the crest are noticeably steeper and more exposed than everything below, and published descriptions hedge them as possibly low fifth class. A rope is advised for anyone staying directly on the crest, and a small rack is enough for what protection there is. The documented route-finding trap is here: parties that drift too high and too far right below the summit get cliffed out and have had to rappel to get back on line, so re-read the description before committing to a line on this section.

climbing_route.label: South-side gully bypass
climbing_route.notes: The alternative to the steep upper crest is to traverse around onto the south side of the ridge — across a snowfield whose presence depends entirely on the season — and scramble one of the southern gullies to the summit. This avoids the exposed final crest but is only straightforward when the traverse snow is in reasonable condition; late season it can be bare and loose, and the choice between the two finishes should be made from what is actually visible on the day.

climbing_route.label: Lower runnels and couloirs
climbing_route.notes: From camp below the face the route links a series of runnels and couloirs for roughly 2,000 vertical feet. It is a spring and early-season objective and the whole face is condition-dependent; the only published account of this line is the first ascent, and it compares the undertaking in scope to the long-standing north face route on Dragontail. Anything written about this face should be read as a description of one party's conditions, not a reliable annual expectation.

climbing_route.label: Water-ice ramp
climbing_route.notes: The defining section is a ramp holding roughly 600 vertical feet of water ice reported at WI2 to WI3. Protection is the documented problem: the first-ascent party carried only two ice screws alongside a rack of rock gear and found that badly short for the ice actually encountered. Carry a real screw rack. Rock protection on this section is described as scarce.

climbing_route.label: Upper snowfields
climbing_route.notes: Above the ice the angle relents into snowfields that lead toward the summit ridge. These snowfields sit above the ice pitches and are the source of the face's main objective hazard — spindrift funnels down the runnels below, and accounts of this face record near-constant spindrift bombardment during and after storm. Spindrift avalanches also swept the face during the first-ascent party's descent.

climbing_route.label: Exit step to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A short ice step reported at about AI2 exits the snowfields near the summit. Retreat from high on the face is not simple, and the first-ascent party did not reverse the route: they descended the southwest side by a snow gully, downclimbing neve and making two 30 m rappels to reach a col west of the peak, then returned to camp as it began snowing. Plan the descent before committing to the face.

climbing_route.label: Cooney Lake to the southeast ridge
climbing_route.notes: From Cooney Lake at about 7,200 ft the trail continues up for roughly another mile to where it meets the easy southeast ridge of the peak. This is walking on trail and open larch-and-scree slopes; the only real considerations are the altitude, the exposure to weather on a ridge with no shelter, and loose footing on the scree.

climbing_route.label: Southeast ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: The southeast ridge is the standard finish and most descriptions rate it class 1 to 2 — an easy walk-up with straightforward route-finding on the broad crest. Accounts differ on the top end: at least one party travelling the ridge reports a few more exposed class 3 steps, so treat class 2 as the typical case rather than a guarantee, and be ready to pick around a step. In shoulder season the same rock ices over and the scrambling becomes considerably more serious for the grade; snow flurries and rapid cooling are commonly reported here in autumn.

climbing_route.label: Sandy ramp under the overhang
climbing_route.notes: The technical climbing starts where the approach ends, at a sandy ramp running up beneath an overhang toward the right side of the buttress. This is scrambling rather than climbing, but it is sandy over rock and is the start of the fall line for anything dislodged above — the ground below this point is described as a rockfall zone and parties downclimb or rappel out of it rather than lingering.

climbing_route.label: Exposed ridge below the summit block
climbing_route.notes: Above the ramp the line follows the ridge with several exposed fourth-class moves leading to the base of the summit block. The recurring hazard reported here is loose rock: large, poised blocks are scattered along the ridgeline, so test holds and keep the party out of each other's fall line. Zig-zagging is characteristic of the route, and long slings are recommended to control rope drag when it is climbed on a rope.

climbing_route.label: Summit-block crux
climbing_route.notes: The crux is a short low-fifth-class sequence on the summit block, generally given around 5.4 for the route overall. The published sequence reaches well out left to a flake and uses the narrow ledge above it as a handhold. Accounts of the summit block also record a small, old and visibly rusty bolt low on a friction slab with essentially no other gear available on that section, so the protection is thin and the bolt should not be trusted as a running belay. Sticky rubber is repeatedly recommended for this bit. Small cams to about 2 inches plus stoppers is the reported rack.

climbing_route.label: Thin ramp to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Above the crux a thin ramp trends east and reaches the roomy summit with one last fourth-class move. Descent is by rappelling the route rather than by any walk-off: three rappels with a single 60 m rope is the reported configuration — one from the end of the technical climbing to a bolted belay ledge, one from chains down the face trending skier's left which just barely reaches third-class ground, and one from a large boulder wrapped in webbing down to the talus. Carry spare webbing; the anchors are old and the slings periodically need replacing.

climbing_route.label: Moat entry to the notch
climbing_route.notes: The climbing starts at the notch in the jagged ridge below the false summit, at roughly 7,200-7,250 ft. Gaining it means a traverse on hard snow around a small moat where the glacier meets the rock, and in many years this shallow rock-and-ice moat is the crux of the whole outing. Reports vary on gear: some parties manage with an ice axe alone on firm snow, others want crampons, and the moat opens up as the season goes on. There is a documented alternative — drop 100 to 200 ft lower and climb a rock finger to reach the same notch — which is worth knowing about before committing to the snow. The rock immediately by the glacier is glacier-polished and slick.

climbing_route.label: Rib traverse and left edge of the ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the notch an exposed traverse around a rib gains the climbable side of the summit block, then the route follows the left edge of the ridge for roughly 160 feet. The position is airy and it looks worse from the false summit than it is; the terrain is third class.

climbing_route.label: Ledge west to the corner and the slot
climbing_route.notes: A ledge is crossed west (left) to a wide corner. The crux of the rock is a short V-shaped slot here, described as a shade harder than the surrounding third-class ground. The rock on the summit block is greenstone and is generally reported as solid and pleasant, but loose material is present and old ring pitons found on route are a reminder that this is not a maintained line. Parties commonly put a rope on for this slot on the way down rather than on the way up, which is where the exposure is felt.

climbing_route.label: Ledges to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Easy ledges above the slot lead over the false summit ground and on to the true summit — an exposed but consistently third-class scramble. The block looks steep and intimidating from the false summit and repeatedly turns out to be easier than it appears. The real risks on this route are the moat crossing below and the descent, not the summit scramble.

climbing_route.label: Debris fan and the bergschrund
climbing_route.notes: The couloir is entered from the fan at its base above Trapper Lake. The basin here collects avalanche debris from the surrounding walls and the South Glacier — accounts describe large trees, house-sized boulders and chunks of ice piled in the runout — which is both a nuisance to walk through and a statement about what comes down this feature. A substantial moat or bergschrund sits at the bottom of the chute and has to be negotiated on the way in and out; it grows through the season. Most parties boot straight up the fan rather than trying to skin through the debris.

climbing_route.label: Lower couloir
climbing_route.notes: The lower couloir runs at a moderate angle and the snow in it is unusually well preserved, because the feature faces north and the surrounding walls are high enough to keep it shaded. The reported pattern is soft snow over a firm crust lens on the sides of the couloir, with deeper unconsolidated snow in the gut, so travel is generally easier on the flanks than up the middle.

climbing_route.label: Sustained mid-couloir
climbing_route.notes: The average angle of the couloir is in the mid-40s, but the middle section holds sustained pitches in the 50s with serious consequence below — a slip here runs the length of the couloir. Sluff runs fast on new snow and needs actively managing. The documented practice is to alternate between the two sides to limit time under overhead hazard. Rock quality on this mountain is described as poor and rockfall is a stated concern in the couloir even by parties who did not see any; a helmet and an early start on frozen snow both follow from that.

climbing_route.label: Upper couloir and top-out
climbing_route.notes: The last 500 vertical feet are reported as the hardest part of the climb, with the crust becoming more pronounced and the surface bumpy near the top. No reliable published description of the finish onto the true summit was found: the accounts available here topped out the couloir and turned around rather than continuing to the summit, so treat the ground above the couloir as unknown and plan accordingly. Warming is the other timing constraint — wet slides off the surrounding cliffy faces are reported through the day, and the exit back out of the Trapper Lake basin toward the col is itself in avalanche terrain.

wa_white_mountain_olympics_scramble.skip_reason: Research turned up only the overall grade (class 2 by its easiest route), the peak's position about 1.5 miles south of Anderson Pass, and approach/elevation-gain figures (roughly 4,000 ft of gain over an 8-mile round-trip scramble day from a Honeymoon Meadows camp). No source was found that describes the actual line of the summit scramble — which slope or ridge is taken, the terrain on it, or its hazards. Writing segments here would mean inventing them, so the section is left empty.
